prime.problem: Zero to Hero never stops to teach its tools. Lecture 1 assumes Python classes and calculus, and from Lecture 2 on a single line such as loss = F.cross_entropy(h @ W2 + b2, Y) uses a matmul, broadcasting, softmax, a log and the chain rule at once. If one of them is shaky, you can't tell a bug in your code from a gap in the math.
prime.fits: This is the front page of course 1. It comes after the start-here map (z2h-0) and before micrograd. It fits the twelve toolkit cards onto one training step: a layer, a loss and its gradient. Every later course repeats that step, so their cards point back to its parts here.
expect: the loss formula: softmax of XW + b, then the average −log p
shapes first: matmul, dims, views and broadcasting
gradients: local slopes multiplied along a chain and added across paths
sampling from p with a seeded generator
prime.goal: Point at any symbol in the loss formula and name the card behind it, predict what each lever in the table does to a number, and check off the six finish conditions before you start micrograd.

attend: Which symbols in the three-line formula come from which card group, and which two cards don't appear in the formula at all?
In the levers table, which mistakes raise an error and which ones just change a number? Why is the second kind more dangerous?
In the sketch, which three operations move numbers without doing arithmetic, and which of them costs memory?
Why does the backward arrow run the whole length of the step, when each card only ever worked out one local slope?
Before any training, which two numbers tell you a fresh model is set up correctly, and which cards predict them?

must: A neuron is a dot product → put examples in the rows of X and neurons in the columns of W → one matmul computes a whole layer, z = XW + b, with b broadcast down the rows → the shapes decide what gets computed, so a shape that fits the wrong way (a missing keepdim) gives wrong numbers and no error

Each output adds up fan_in products → independent variances add, so the std grows like √fan_in (3.16 at fan_in 10) → dividing W by √fan_in keeps the logits near std 1 → softmax stays soft and the loss at step 0 starts near log 27 = 3.2958

Logits can have any sign → softmax exponentiates and normalises, and only the gaps between logits matter → the loss is −log p(correct), averaged over the batch → working in logs avoids float32 underflow (a product of 0.0 vs a log-sum of −3295.84) and ranks models the same way

Each operation knows its own local slope → the chain rule multiplies slopes along a path and adds across paths → one backward sweep gives ∂L/∂W for every weight → check it with a nudge at a moderate h (about 10⁻⁵), and use += so a value used twice keeps both paths
elevated: A seed fixes one generator's stream, not every device's → the CPU generator replays the notebook's [0.7081, 0.3542, 0.1054] while mps gives [0.9843, …] → the makemore labs stay on cpu so that every "you should see" matches
reference: the exact dunder names (__rmul__, __radd__) and the build_topo code
the seven derivative rules as a table
the venv install commands and package versions

compress.prompt: Card closed. Draw the whole course's causal map on one page. Start from a batch X and end at ∂L/∂W. Write the formula, place all twelve cards on it by number, and draw an arrow for every "because" (for example: variances add → divide W by √fan_in → the first loss is near 3.2958). Circle the arrows where a mistake runs silently.
checklist: z = XW + b: a matmul (7), with shapes read first (8) and b broadcast down the rows (9); one entry is a dot product (6)
W scaled by 1/√fan_in, because variances add (11)
softmax, then −log p(correct) averaged (12), all done in logs to avoid underflow (5)
backward: local slopes (3), multiplied along the chain and added across paths (4)
p also feeds sampling with a seeded multinomial (10); Python (1) and the setup (2) are what it all runs on
the silent mistakes circled: a missing keepdim, unscaled W, softmax before F.cross_entropy, = instead of +=

retrieve.q: Explain where the 3.2958 in the formula's key comes from, using only the softmax and log cards, and why it is the loss you expect from a well-initialised 27-class model before training.
answer: equal (for example all-zero) logits make softmax uniform: p = 1/27 for every class
the loss is −log(1/27) = log 27 = 3.2958, whatever the target
a good init keeps the logits small, so the step-0 loss lands near it
a step-0 loss far above it means the logits are too large: confidently wrong (28.29 with an unscaled 200-input output layer)

retrieve.q: Walk one batch of 32 three-character contexts through the formula to the loss and back. At each step, name the card and say what happens to the shape.
answer: X (32, 3) integers → C[X] (32, 3, 2), a lookup that copies
.view(-1, 6) → (32, 6), relabelled without copying
@ W1 (6, 100) + b1 (100,) → (32, 100): a matmul, with b broadcast down the rows
then logits (32, 27) → softmax along each row → pick p[n, y<sub>n</sub>] → −log, mean → one number
backward: local slopes multiplied along the chain; b's gradient is summed over the 32 rows it was stretched across

retrieve.q: You suspect a bug in a hand-written gradient. Compare checking it with a nudge and checking it against torch autograd: what does each cost, and when does each mislead you?
answer: a nudge needs one extra forward pass per input and is only approximate
a big h leaves the curvature term (14.3 at h = 0.1), and a tiny h is swamped by round-off (14.0012 at 10⁻¹²); use about 10⁻⁵, or the centred difference
autograd is exact and does every input in one backward pass, but it only helps if you compare against it (0.141302 vs the nudge's 0.141301)
neither catches a mistake in the forward formula itself

retrieve.q: A teammate wants to move the makemore labs to device='mps' because a matmul was 2.5× faster there. What do you gain, what do you lose, and what do you recommend?
answer: gain: 27.4 ms → 10.9 ms in one run, but only 14.4 → 8.5 ms (1.7×) in a quieter one
lose: the mps generator runs a different stream, so seeded draws, losses and samples stop matching the notebooks
the makemore nets are small: the longest makemore run is 301 s on the cpu
keep cpu for makemore, and use mps for the GPT lectures

compare.q: The whole-stack card draws the series as a factory line on which backprop and the training loop never change. Which part of that line does this course already contain in miniature, and what does the line need that no toolkit card provides?
answer: the constant core is here: a layer, softmax, −log p and the chain rule back to the weights
what changes from station to station (context 1 → 3 → 8 → 256) is mostly X's shape and what sits between X and the logits, and the shape cards handle that
missing: learning itself. The toolkit computes ∂L/∂W but never updates W, so there's no learning rate and no training loop yet
that update, w ← w − lr·∂L/∂w, is what micrograd (z2h-2) adds

compare.q: The big-ideas card splits the toolkit into six claims, and this overview joins it into one formula. What does each view make easy to see, and which kind of question would you answer from each?
answer: the claims isolate mechanisms (why slopes multiply, why √n), which is good for "why does this work?"
the formula shows how the pieces interact: init scale → logit size → step-0 loss
so the formula is the one to debug a pipeline with, and the levers table attaches a measured number to each part
use the claims to explain, and the formula to locate a fault

predict.q: The toolkit gave you seven local rules and the chain rule, but you applied them by hand. The small network at the end of Lecture 1 has 41 parameters. Commit before revealing: what must each number remember so that a program can find all 41 gradients for you, and how many passes does that take compared with nudging?
predict.answer: Its parents, the operation that made it, and a closure holding its local slope. One forward pass then records the graph, and one backward sweep in reversed topological order gives every gradient exactly. Nudging would need 41 extra forward passes, each only approximate. That's micrograd's Value, and its whole engine is 94 lines. Start with the Value object.

apply.task: Break the pipeline three ways, one at a time, and write down the symptom you expect before running each. (1) Normalise the 3×3 counts N = [[1, 1, 2], [3, 0, 1], [6, 2, 2]] with N / N.sum(1). (2) Compute y = x @ w for x (1000, 10) and w (10, 200), both plain torch.randn, then again with w / 10**0.5. (3) Call F.cross_entropy(F.softmax(logits, 1), y) for logits [[2.0, 1.0, 0.1]] and y = [0]. For each one, name the card it belongs to and say whether PyTorch raised an error.
apply.done: (1) The row sums are [0.7, 0.85, 2.2] instead of 1.0 each. (2) y's std is about 3.16, then about 1.0. (3) The loss is 0.8021 instead of 0.4170. None of the three raises an error, which is the point.
apply.hint: For each bug, decide which one number would expose it: a row sum, a std, or the loss of an example you already know.
